# navit

**Offline turn-by-turn navigation that follows the GPS, with spoken directions**

- **Version recorded:** 0.5.6
- **Categories:** `gps-gnss`, `navigation-maps`
- **Upstream:** <https://www.navit-project.org/>
- **Needs first:** `gpsd`

## What it does

A navigation program for a laptop or a cyberdeck: a moving map that follows your position from gpsd, routes to an address or a point you pick on the map, and speaks the turns through espeak-ng. It reads maps from files on the disk, so once the maps are installed nothing it does needs a network. With no destination set it is a situational display: the map follows the GPS and shows position and speed.

## Why you would want it

A phone's navigation needs the phone network for its maps and often for its routing, which is the thing that is missing in a field deployment, at a remote site or after a storm. Navit with the maps already on the machine keeps working. It is the offline alternative to phone or web navigation, and it shares the same gpsd feed as APRS, grid-square and time tools rather than taking the receiver for itself.

## Before it will work

A GPS receiver served by gpsd (the `gpsd` unit, installed first), and maps: the `osm-regions` and `osm-navit` units, which need your regions set first with `hammunition station set --map-regions`. The launcher runs `hammunition maps navit`, which opens the configuration `osm-navit` writes, so it has nothing to open until `osm-navit` has installed. A repeater layer from `hammunition maps repeaters import` is added to a copy of it in your own data directory, which the launcher then opens. Spoken directions need working audio output.

## How it installs

- apt: `navit`, `navit-gui-internal`, `navit-graphics-gtk-drawing-area`, `espeak-ng`, `maptool`

## Known problems

The internal GUI is built for a touch screen: its menus are large tiles opened by clicking the map, and there is no menu bar, which surprises anyone expecting a desktop application. The launcher's configuration is not edited by hand: it is generated from Debian's /etc/navit/navit.xml with the speech set to espeak-ng and the installed maps added, and it is rewritten on every install, so a change made to it is lost. Your own ~/.navit directory, which holds bookmarks and the last destination, is never touched. Whether Navit routes across two separately converted regions, such as a trip from one state into the next, has not yet been measured on hardware.
